Amalekites
uh-MAL-eh-kytes
proper noun (a perpetual enemy of Israel)
From Amalek, grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:12); the desert people who attacked Israel after the exodus and became the standing emblem of the unrelenting enemy of God's people.

Biblical Definition

The Amalekites were a nomadic desert people, descended from Amalek the grandson of Esau, who became the archetypal enemy of Israel and of the LORD. They attacked Israel from behind soon after the exodus, smiting the feeble and weary at the rear when the people were faint, and fearing not God. For this the LORD swore that He would have war with Amalek from generation to generation and would utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; Moses built an altar and called it Jehovah-nissi, “the LORD my banner.” Centuries later the LORD charged Saul to execute that long-deferred sentence, to smite Amalek and utterly destroy all that they had; but Saul spared Agag the king and the best of the spoil, and for this disobedience the kingdom was rent from him. Haman the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews in Esther, sprang from this same line. The dictionary marks the Amalekites as the standing figure of the implacable foe that fears not God and strikes at the weak—and of the sin that, spared rather than slain, returns to threaten the people of God. Saul's partial obedience is the perpetual warning: to spare what God has devoted to destruction is rebellion, for to obey is better than sacrifice. The flesh, like Amalek, is to be given no quarter; what God commands to be put to death is not to be kept alive for the sake of the best of the spoil.

Webster 1828 Definition

The desert people, descended from Esau's grandson Amalek, who attacked Israel's weak and weary after the exodus; the archetypal God-defying enemy under perpetual divine sentence (Exodus 17:16), spared by Saul to his ruin.

AMALEKITES, proper noun. A nomadic desert people descended from Amalek, grandson of Esau.

They attacked Israel's feeble and weary rear after the exodus, fearing not God (Deuteronomy 25:18).

The LORD swore perpetual war with Amalek and to blot out its remembrance (Exodus 17:16).

Saul was charged to destroy them utterly, but spared Agag and the spoil (1 Samuel 15:3).

The archetype of the implacable enemy of God and His people; Haman the Agagite sprang from them.

Key Scripture

Ex 17:16 — "For he said, Because the LORD hath sworn that the LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."

De 25:17 — "Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt;"

De 25:18 — "How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God."

1 Sa 15:3 — "Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the live danger is the recoil from the herem (devotion to destruction) that would charge God with cruelty, missing both His long forbearance and the figure of unspared sin.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the justice of God in the devoting of Amalek to destruction. Modern sentiment recoils from the command to utterly destroy, charging it with cruelty. The dictionary answers that the sentence fell after centuries of forbearance upon a people who, unprovoked, struck the weak and weary of Israel and feared not God; the LORD's patience ran long before His justice fell. The herem was not genocide for land or gain but the righteous judgment of the holy God upon an implacable and God-defying foe, executed by His express command.

The account also yields a perpetual lesson in the partial obedience that ruins. Saul smote Amalek but spared Agag and the best of the spoil, and called his rebellion sacrifice. Samuel's verdict stands: to obey is better than sacrifice, and rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft. The dictionary reads Amalek as a figure of the flesh and of besetting sin: what God has devoted to death is to be slain wholly, not kept alive for the sake of the best of the spoil, for the sin we spare will, like Amalek, return to war against us from generation to generation.

Hebrew Roots

From Amalek (Hebrew 'Amaleq), grandson of Esau by Eliphaz (Genesis 36:12); a desert people of the Negeb and Sinai, kin to Edom and perennial foe of Israel.

expand to see more

'Amaleq, the grandson of Esau, eponymous ancestor of the people.

A nomadic people of the Negeb and the Sinai wilderness.

Cherem, Hebrew, the “devotion to destruction” commanded against them.

Jehovah-nissi, “the LORD my banner,” the altar Moses named after the victory (Exodus 17:15).

Agag their king, whence Haman “the Agagite” of the book of Esther.

Usage

"The teacher defended the judgment on Amalek as righteous, falling after long divine forbearance."

"He preached Saul's sparing of Agag as the warning against partial obedience that calls rebellion sacrifice."

"She read Amalek as a figure of besetting sin, to be slain wholly and not spared for the best of the spoil."
